ARTnews.com https://www.artnews.com The Leading Source for Art News & Art Event Coverage Tue, 04 Aug 2026 19:06:07 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.5 https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-artnews-2019/assets/app/icons/favicon.png ARTnews.com https://www.artnews.com 32 32 168890962 Guggenheim Veteran Valerie Hillings Tapped as Inaugural Director of Abu Dhabi Branch https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/valerie-hillings-director-guggenheim-abu-dhabi-1234794298/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 19:06:06 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794298

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi took another significant step toward its December 11 opening, naming Valerie Hillings as the institution’s inaugural director.

In choosing Hillings, the Guggenheim tapped a trusted name for the high-profile appointment. She spent five years on the Guggenheim’s staff in New York before joining the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi project in 2008 as curator and associate director of curatorial affairs. She worked alongside the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi through 2018, laying the groundwork for its acquisition strategy and curatorial focus on art from West Asia, North Africa, and South Asia from 1960 onward. 

“I am honored to return to Abu Dhabi to complete the once-in-a-lifetime journey of founding and opening Guggenheim Abu Dhabi,” Hillings said in a statement. “I look forward to welcoming local and global audiences to the magnificent Frank Gehry-designed building and inviting them to explore points of interconnection and unique stories.”

Hillings returns to Abu Dhabi after an eight-year tenure as director of the North Carolina Museum of Art (NCMA) in Raleigh. During her tenure, the museum’s attendance grew to 1.2 million annual visitors, and she oversaw the rehang of its permanent collection for the first time in more than a decade, under the title “The People’s Collection, Reimagined.” She also expanded NCMA’s collection by roughly 400 works, including adding the museum’s first Pablo Picasso painting.

Hillings holds a doctorate in art history from New York University’s Institute of Fine Arts and a degree in art history from Duke University. In 2014, she curated “Zero: Countdown to Tomorrow, 1950s–60s” at the Guggenheim New York, a landmark survey of the experimental postwar German group Zero.

Upon its opening, Hillings will oversee the largest branch in the Guggenheim’s four-country museum network and the most eagerly awaited addition to the Saadiyat Cultural District. Plans for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi were announced in 2006, and the ensuing two decades of delays and controversies have brought the project to completion at a reported cost of roughly $1 billion. The museum comprises 30 galleries, spanning 11,600 square meters (124,860 square feet) of interior exhibition space and 23,000 square meters (247,570 square feet) of outdoor exhibition space. 

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi sits within walking distance of the Louvre Abu Dhabi, which opened in 2017, as well as the more recently inaugurated Zayed National Museum and Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi. According to Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of DCT Abu Dhabi, the new Guggenheim will represent “a defining moment in our cultural journey.”

]]> 1234794298 A Colossal Ancient Marble Statue Emerges at a UNESCO Site in Turkey https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/colossal-ancient-marble-statue-emerges-unesco-site-turkey-1234794286/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 18:31:30 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794286

A seven-foot-tall marble statue from the 5th century BCE has emerged from under what used to be a Roman roadway in the ancient city of Sardis, in western Turkey, reports Heritage Daily. A UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Salihli district of Manisa Province, the city served at the time as the capital of the western satrapy of the Achaemenid Persian empire and of the kingdom of Lydia.

According to Turkey’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, who posted about the discovery on Facebook, the sculpture, dated between 470 and 450 BCE, is one of the rare surviving examples of monumental marble statuary from the period. After conservation work is complete, the statue will go on view at Turkey’s Manisa Museum. The dig is under the administration of the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums.

Discovered in two large parts, the sculpture is missing its feet and some other fragments. During the Roman period, it had been repurposed and placed under paving material—which, ironically, allowed for its facial features and other details to be well preserved. 

Experts say that the sculpture is stylistically hybrid, with an upright stance and long hair that were current in the 6th century BCE and a treatment of the face and hands that reflects trends in the first half of the 5th century BCE.

The figure wears a thick himation (an ancient Greek cloak or wrap) and a chiton (a rectangular tunic) over a distinctive horizontally striped garment. Experts point out that there are no known examples of this sort of clothing in comparable sculptures from Anatolia or mainland Greece, so the garb reflects a local tradition distinct to the ancient kingdom of Lydia.

The figure holds what may be a quince in its right hand, possibly an offering to a deity. From this feature, archaeologists hope to learn more about ritual practices and religious beliefs in the city.

Sardis became famous for its wealth under King Croesus, points out Greek Reporter, which notes that the artwork may provide new insight into cultural exchange between the Greek, Lydian, and Persian worlds.

]]> 1234794286 Sale of Insolvent Glasgow Art Center’s Archive Would Be an ‘Irreversible Loss,’ Critics Warn https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/glasgow-cca-archive-sale-creative-scotland-1234794285/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 18:15:41 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794285

Campaigners, politicians, and arts figures are calling on the Scottish government to intervene over the possible sale of the archive of Glasgow’s Centre for Contemporary Arts, according to The Art Newspaper. The collection was listed among the assets of the Centre for Contemporary Arts (CCA), which was recently deemed insolvent.

The collapse came despite a significant injection of public money. The BBC reported in January that the CCA had secured more than $4.5 million in three-year funding from Creative Scotland only a year before its closure. The organization had been struggling for years, however. It was forced to close for six months after the 2018 Glasgow School of Art fire, temporarily shut again in late 2024 over financial concerns and became embroiled in disputes with pro-Palestinian artists over calls for the center to boycott Israel. 

By January, Creative Scotland said the CCA could no longer show that it was financially viable, and its board acknowledged it had couldn’t to find a sustainable financial footing.

The archive, which also includes material from the CCA’s predecessor, the Third Eye Centre, holds more than 50 years of cultural activity in Glasgow through exhibition records, photographs, posters, films, flyers and other ephemera. Its inclusion among the CCA’s assets has sparked bnot just protests but also a petition calling for the collection to remain intact. 

Creative Scotland, which owns the CCA building, said it is working with Glasgow Life and the Ballast Trust, an archives charity, to find ways to preserve the collection and keep it publicly accessible in Glasgow. 

Amanda Catto, a former portfolio manager at Creative Scotland, described the archive as “part of Scotland’s cultural memory” and warned that breaking it up or selling it would represent “an irreversible loss to Scotland’s cultural record.” She also raised concerns about what the episode could mean for archives held by other cultural organizations that might run into financial trouble. 

MB Valuations, which was instructed to dispose of its assets, is seeking advice about the archive and inviting expressions of interest rather than including it in the broader auction of the center’s furniture and equipment. The firm reportedly hopes the collection can remain together under institutional ownership. 

The dispute follows the collapse of the CCA earlier this year after a prolonged period of financial problem. The organization entered liquidation in January, resulting in the loss of all its staff, and Creative Scotland subsequently announced plans to sell the building, which had served as a major center for contemporary art in Scotland for more than two decades. 

The Office of the Scottish Charity Regulator opened an inquiry into the CCA’s financial governance following its collapse but concluded the investigation last week without taking further action.

]]> 1234794285 Terran Last Gun’s Antique Accounting Ledgers Tell New Stories https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/columns/terran-last-gun-new-talent-2026-1234794280/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:11:43 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794280

Growing up in the Pacific Northwest, my first border crossing on foot was from the US into Canada. I remember getting the jitters as I offered up my passport—and then it was over in the flick of a turnstile. Terran Last Gun (Piikani) grew up on Montana’s Blackfeet Indian Reservation, less than an hour’s drive away, but rarely made the same crossing in his youth. 

During Western expansion, the border line grew in phases along the 49th parallel and eventually divided the rangelands of Last Gun’s ancestors, whose kin now live on both sides. Early on, in the mid-19th century, the Blackfoot people traversed it freely, evading the US Army by weaving into British territory. For this alleviating effect, they called it the Medicine Line. These days, moving within the same territory involves “a lot of showing your papers,” as Last Gun said he has heard from Blackfeet friends.

Last Gun’s studio in Santa Fe, New Mexico, is stacked with the literal receipts of this annexation in the form of antique accounting ledgers, many of them from Montana. In tight cursive, they document the surge of a settler colonial grid over the Great Plains, as well as all sorts of micro-histories therein. “There was a note in one of them,” Last Gun said. “Somebody had erased it, but I could still read it. It was like a crime report—it said, ‘He beat her.’” 

Using ink and colored pencils, Last Gun applies crisp geometric forms to sheets he excises from the tomes he collects. Some of the fields are Ellsworth Kelly–flat; others reveal the thousands of strokes that overtake tidy ledger cells. The underlying grids hold such extreme historical tension that adding anything to them feels charged, opening up an unlikely, unemphatic space for the artist to play. 

Last Gun pulls in visual motifs related to Blackfoot lodges, hides, and war shirts, excerpted and stylized so as not to reveal “too much” of their sacred contexts. (“Sometimes I wish I could share more,” he said.) He also references color-field painters and printmakers from his studies at Santa Fe’s Institute of American Indian Arts, from which he graduated with a museum studies degree in 2016. Last year, for Site Santa Fe’s latest biennial, he completed a series inspired by the Transcendental Painting Group, a short-lived Southwest collective whose atmospheric abstractions radiate heartbreaking pre-World War II optimism.

Last Gun’s work is a departure from ledger art, a Plains Indian tradition in which late 19th-century artists adapted to reservation confinement by making narrative art on ledgers instead of hides. Historical examples largely feature figurative imagery on blank sheets, whereas Last Gun tends toward geometrics that evoke midcentury architecture, vaporware desktop art—and cheerful censor bars.

During our studio visit, Last Gun lifted a ledger sheet toward a window to reveal its watermark. “They’re craft objects in themselves,” he said of a set of pages from Blaine County in northern Montana—ancestral Blackfeet territory, but not part of the reservation. “My people didn’t have access to these documents,” Last Gun said. “These were dark times. It’s really interesting that I have access now.” He likened the feeling to holding a reclaimed piece of Montana in his hands.

]]> 1234794280 Art Week NYC Names 76 Participating Galleries for Inaugural Event in November https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/art-week-nyc-names-2026-participating-galleries-list-1234794276/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:46:42 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794276

On Tuesday, Art Week NYC, the soon-to-launch annual citywide celebration of contemporary art presented by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum, announced the galleries participating in its gallery program.

Seventy-six galleries are set to participate in the inaugural edition of the event, set to take place November 11–14. Among those participating are blue-chip enterprises like Hauser & Wirth, Gagosian, David Zwirner, Pace Gallery, White Cube, Perrotin, Lisson, and Paula Cooper. Other galleries run the gamut from emerging to midsize, and are located across the city’s gallery districts, including Chelsea, Tribeca, the Lower East Side, and the Upper East Side.

“Our vision for Art Week NYC began with the galleries,” Danielle McConnell, publisher of Artforum, said in a statement. “The galleries are where artists are discovered, careers are built, and the conversation around contemporary art moves forward. By bringing them together under one citywide platform, we’re creating an experience that reflects the strength and diversity of New York’s gallery community. We’re excited to invite audiences to see art where it is best seen, at the galleries and museums across the city.” 

In addition to the gallery program, ARTnews will present the Art Week NYC Hub, with a full slate of live interviews, panel discussions, artist talks, and other editorial programming to be announced in hte coming months. Artforum and the New Museum will also host a day of public programming, and the ADAA Fair will present its 2026 edition during the event.

“Every day, ARTnews reports on the continuous changes in today’s art ecosystem.  The collector base needs to grow through education and experience. To complement the galleries’ programs, ARTnews will host a series of conversations that highlight the many ways to love and support art. We will also explore how art intersects with the worlds of sports, music, and fashion,” said ARTnews publisher Erica Lubow Necarsulmer. “ARTnews’s curated conversations will welcome art lovers at every stage of their journey in a compelling yet approachable format.”

]]> 1234794276 London Mayor Defends Free Entry to Museums, UK’s National Gallery Criticized, and More: Morning Links for August 4, 2026 https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/london-mayor-defends-free-entry-to-museums-morning-links-1234794277/ Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:24:49 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794277

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • The National Gallery has been criticized after spending £250,000 on its NG Citizens program.
  • Royal Museums Greenwich staff have voted for industrial action over pay, conditions, and workplace reforms.
  • London’s mayor has defended free entry to the capital’s national museums, arguing that culture should remain accessible regardless of income or background.

The Headlines

LAND OF THE FREE. London mayor Sadiq Khan has defended free entry to the capital’s national museums, arguing that culture should remain accessible regardless of income or background. In an op-ed for LBC, Khan said free admission transformed museum access, with visits rising significantly after charges were removed, while also boosting tourism and making museums vital public spaces. His comments come amid renewed debate over proposals to charge overseas visitors at England’s national museums. Supporters argue tourist fees could help address funding pressures, while critics warn they risk undermining the principle of museums as institutions open to all.

‘BARKING MAD.’ The UK’s National Gallery has been criticized after spending £250,000 on NG Citizens, a five-year citizens’ assembly designed to help shape the museum’s future, the Times of London reported. Fifty people, selected through a civic lottery to reflect the UK’s diversity—including some with no art background—will advise on the gallery’s priorities, though not acquisitions or curatorial decisions. Critics, including art experts and Conservative MP Charlie Dewhirst, argue the initiative undermines professional expertise and call it “barking mad.” The gallery says the project is about strengthening public engagement and ensuring its future reflects a broader cross-section of society, not replacing expert decision-making.

The Digest

UNESCO has been urged to investigate feared damage to Lebanon’s World Heritage–listed Beaufort Castle after the Israeli military triggered explosions nearby. [The Art Newspaper]

A Scottish architect has launched a petition calling for the Mackintosh Building at the Glasgow School of Art, twice devastated by fire, to be fully restored and transferred to an independent organization. [Artnet News]

Museum strikes are spreading across London as Royal Museums Greenwichstaff have voted for industrial action over pay, conditions, and workplace reforms. [Artforum]

An anonymous Belgian collector has loaned a rare René Magritte work to the Israel Museum as the artist’s iconic The Castle of the Pyrenees undergoes restoration after accidental damage. [Jerusalem Post]

The Kicker

PULLING BACK THE CURTAIN. A new BBC series called The Big Deal with Steph McGovern aims to pull back the curtain on the art market, exploring how artworks are discovered, valued, and sold. The six-part competition kicks off on August 13 and follows aspiring dealers as they navigate the business of buying and selling contemporary art, testing their instincts, commercial skills, and ability to spot emerging talent. The series seeks to challenge perceptions of the art world as exclusive or inaccessible.

]]> 1234794277 Francisco Correa Cordero, Founder of Closely Watched New York Gallery Lubov, Dies https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/francisco-correa-cordero-lubov-gallery-dead-1234794249/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 22:12:51 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794249

Francisco Correa Cordero, the founder of New York gallery Lubov, died on August 2. The news was announced in a post on the gallery’s Instagram account, which did not provide a cause or age.

“He accomplished and lived for his dream through the gallery of a safe and meaningful community for artists – what he built through Lubov will be felt through the art community forever,” the gallery’s post reads, which notes that Correa Cordero “passed away peacefully surrounded by what he loved the most – his chosen family, laughter and so much love.”

Lubov did not immediately return ARTnews’s request for comment. A pinned Instagram post from February 2025, featuring a Photoshopped “WANTED” poster for the dealer, lists his birthday as July 14, 1989, which means he would have been 37.

The gallery’s currently website lists a solo show for Kane Huynh for the fall, with its most recent exhibition having been a solo for Adelisa Selimbašić, which closed on June 21.  

Correa Cordero opened Lubov in November 2016 in a second-floor unit at 373 Broadway in Tribeca, long before the neighborhood became a blue-chip gallery neighborhood. In 2019, Lubov moved to a fourth-floor space at 5 East Broadway, on the border of the Lower East Side and Chinatown, with the opening show being a solo for José Manuel Mesías, presented by Havana’s El Apartamento as part of Condo.

The gallery’s first-ever show was a solo for Chicago-based artist Boris Ostrerov, which was also his first New York solo show. In the years that followed, Lubov would become known for its eclectic mix of exhibitions, from single- and two-artist shows to group exhibitions, with both rising artists and well-known names, including Marsha Pels, Andres Serrano, My Barbarian, Eunnam Hong, Covey Gong, Parker Ito, Mimi Park, Shannon Cartier Lucy, and Mira Dayal. The gallery’s exhibitions would often be featured by several publications, including the New York Times, New York, Artforum, ARTnews, Art in America, Bomb, and Interview.

“Francisco supported my first solo gallery show in New York, and so clearly trusted my vision for the installation from the start,“ Dayal told ARTnews in an email. “I wanted to work with him specifically because he was one of the few people supporting labor-intensive, site-specific, and commercially irreverent work, and he was also kind and curious. It is particularly challenging to run that kind of program, especially while also working for another organization, and so it was exciting to see how he expanded the gallery and its community over the years—I specifically remember the enthusiasm over his first show of Shannon Cartier Lucy’s work, his temporary hair salon, and his excellent show with Mimi Park. Years after we worked together, he still showed so much support for me and my work. I’m sure he will be missed by so many artists.”

For the NADA Miami fair in 2022, the gallery described itself as “support[ing] the production and exhibition of new work by emerging artists through commissions and solo exhibitions,” adding, “By connecting different generations with multiple perspectives, and from various regions in the world, Lubov is committed to promoting overlooked practices and experimental approaches.”

Born in Mexico City, Correa Cordero previously worked at galleries such as Exit Art, Martos, and Yancey Richardson before setting out on his own. He also worked as executive coordinator for Independent Curators International (ICI) from 2015 to 2022.

“Francisco was one of the hardest working people I knew, which was something in him that was fueled by passion and endless excitement at the prospect of making the impossible possible,” ICI executive and artistic director Renaud Proch wrote in an email. “He was a dreamer in the best possible ways: he spent hours figuring out how to make something happen, because it needed to happen. His dreaming moved us forward, brought artists out of the shadows, rewarded us with weird, challenging, meaningful, exciting art. His dreaming, like so much of the art he championed, was countercultural; it found a place in our lives even when the conditions for its existence were absent. I honor his courage, I will miss him, and I will always remember his constant beaming, somewhat nervous smile.”

Several artists, curators, and galleries added their remembrances in the comments to the post announcing Correa Cordero’s passing. Margot Norton, chief curator of Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, wrote, “Truly utterly heartbreaking to hear this 💔💔💔 what a brilliant, sensitive champion of artists and wonderful person.” San Juan–based gallery Embajada commented, “We love you Francisco amigo ❤️😢 Rest in Peace🕊️ 😓.”

Artist Dennis Kardon, who had a 2024 solo show at Lubov, wrote, “This is a huge loss. He was the rare gallerist with an authentic intuition for what was heartfelt in work and elevated every artist that drew his interest. The artworld needs people like Francisco to power the engine of contemporary art. His welcoming charm and optimism are rare and he drew in a sophisticated crowd of young (and not so young!) artists and writers. I hope he will live on as a goal for everyone in art to be open and follow their dreams.”

]]> 1234794249 Top 200 Collectors Clara Wu Tsai and Joseph Tsai to Divorce After Nearly 30 Years https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/clara-wu-tsai-joseph-tsai-divorce-1234794234/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 22:04:10 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794234

Clara Wu Tsai and Joseph Tsai, the billionaire art collectors and owners of the Brooklyn Nets and New York Liberty, are divorcing after nearly 30 years of marriage, the New York Post reported Friday.

The couple, who married in New York in 1996, were named jointly to ARTnews’s Top 200 Collectors list in 2018 and 2025, with a focus on contemporary art.

A representative for the Tsais told the Post that the split was mutual and amicable and that the two plan to keep working together across their business and philanthropic interests. Tsai will remain chairman of Brooklyn Sports and Entertainment and governor of the Nets, while Wu Tsai will remain vice chair and governor of the Liberty.

The couple’s art collection is relatively private, but their patronage has been much more visible. In recent years, they have helped bring work by Rashid Johnson, Tavares Strachan, and LaToya Ruby Frazier to Barclays Center, where Nets and Liberty play. In 2025, Frazier showed freestanding portraits of New York Liberty players there in what was her first public art commission.

Wu Tsai told Cultured that year that sports fans and art lovers had something in common: both were looking for “some sort of transcendence,” which made showing art in a sports setting feel natural to her.

Their giving has also reached major New York institutions. In 2022, the pair donated $50 million toward the redevelopment of David Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center, and they have supported exhibitions at the Brooklyn Museum and the Museum of the City of New York. The Tsais also established the Joe and Clara Tsai Foundation in 2014, with work spanning the arts, science, and social justice.

]]> 1234794234 Met Museum Quietly Hangs a Leonardo da Vinci Painting, On Loan from Ken Griffin: ‘A Little Picture, Of Large-Scale Importance’ https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/met-museum-leonardo-da-vinci-ken-griffin-1234794238/ Mon, 03 Aug 2026 21:52:59 +0000 https://www.artnews.com/?p=1234794238

Get ready for Leonardo da Vinci fever at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, where the curators, without so much as a press release, hung a painting this spring by the Renaissance master. On a Monday visit, the work wasn’t gaining any particularly high level of attention as it hung in gallery 609, on the second floor in the European paintings department. The small painting hangs between giant ones by Francesco Francia and Andrea Solario.

Madonna of the Yarnwinder (ca. 1505 per a wall label, ca. 1501 per the museum’s website), attributed on a wall label to the master and his studio, comes from the collection of billionaire hedge funder and ARTnews Top 200 collector Kenneth C. Griffin. (Griffin’s office did not immediately answer an email requesting information on when he acquired the painting.)

Some artworks become known by the name of their past owners; this Leonardo panel is also known as the Lansdowne Madonna, having once belonged to the Marchioness of Lansdowne, in whose collection it was first recorded, in the 19th century, per the wall label. The painting was created for one Florimond Robertet, a French official.

The museum has played the new arrival, the only one by Leonardo on view in its galleries, very close to the vest; it’s been there since spring, but a public-facing museum employee told ARTnews that they heard about it not from the institution but from a friend. This weekend, New York art dealer Evan Beard posted about it on Instagram, which is how ARTnews learned of it; the eagle-eyed reporter Judith Dobrzysnki actually beat him to the punch, posting about it on April 5. According to a museum spokesperson, the work is on long-term loan.

“Who just hangs a Leonardo on the wall like it’s no big deal?” Beard said in a message to ARTnews. “The Met, I guess.” 

It is, to say the least, uncommon to see Leonardo in North America. Most of his paintings hang in the Louvre or Florence’s Uffizi Gallery. The National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., owns his Ginevra de’ Benci (ca. 1474/1478), the only Da Vinci on permanent exhibition in the Americas. It was purchased for a record $5 million in 1967, about $50.8 million in today’s dollars. 

Those figures are still pocket change compared to the $450.3 million brought by his Salvator Mundi (ca. 1500) at Christie’s in 2017, the record for a painting at auction and believed to be the most ever paid for an artwork.

In the Lansdowne Madonna, measuring about 20 inches high, a large Christ child sits on the rocks next to the Virgin Mary, holding and staring at a yarnwinder, a cross-shaped tool (the wall label refers to it as a “niddy-noddy”) used to shape loose skeins of yarn into neat packages; here, it serves to foreshadow the Crucifixion. Another version of it is on view at the National Galleries of Scotland. (That painting was stolen from Drumlanrig Castle, home of its owner, the Duke of Buccleuch, in 2003, at which time it was estimated to be worth £40 million; it remained missing for four years before it was recovered.)

In a 1501 letter to famed Renaissance patron Isabella d’Este, quoted in the wall label, Fra Pietro da Novarellara, head of the Carmelites in Florence, wrote that the artist was working on “a Madonna seated as if she were about to spin yarn. The Child has placed his foot on the basket of yarns and has grasped the yarnwinder and gazes attentively at the four spokes that are in the form of a cross. As if desirous of the cross he smiles and holds it firm, and is unwilling to yield it to his mother who seems to want to take it away from him.”

“No one had previously depicted the Virgin and Child in quite this way,” wrote scholar Martin Kemp in a 2011 catalogue for a National Gallery of Scotland exhibition, “Leonardo da Vinci: The Mystery of the Madonna of the Yarnwinder,” focused on the Buccleuch version. Of the Madonna, he writes that he sees “a clear sense of unease—even of premonition—in her anxious gaze and hovering hand.” Of the symbolism of the cross, he writes, “Leonardo has integrated the meaning of the symbol into the physical and psychological narrative of the painting in a highly innovatory manner,” adding, “This new type of dynamic symbolism was to have a profound effect on the development of High Renaissance art in Florence.” 

The painting would soon become widely known in Italy and elsewhere in Europe, Kemp writes, proving “incredibly popular.” At the time of the 2011 exhibition, the painting was noted to reside in a private collection in New York. Both it and the Buccleuch version, he wrote, have been described as the original. Kemp described the painting hanging at the Met as “one of the two best versions of the Madonna made for Robertet.” It has been variously attributed over the years, he noted, as a copy by a follower, a studio replica, a studio work with “substantial intervention” by Leonardo, and as the original picture. The background is “archteypally Leonardesque,” matching that in other canvases; he identified a bridge in the middle ground as “virtually identical to that on the right of the Mona Lisa.”

In 2011, Kemp wrote that he was “not inclined to recognise Leonardo’s personal touch in the relatively free handling of the landscape, and the forms of the rocks and the mountains seem to lack the rhythmic structuring of his autograph backgrounds.” He went on, however, “At present I prefer to regard the New York picture as completed in the master’s studio rather later than the Buccleuch painting—but executed directly under his control, with his active participation in its design and perhaps also in the actual execution of the figure group.” 

But, he said in a phone interview with ARTnews, he said he has since modified his assessment: “It’s Leonardo and studio.”

“There’s been further technical examination that has shown that it is a picture of complex origins,” said Kemp. “There are Leonardo underdrawings in both pictures, one almost certainly intended for the King of France and the other for a court officer. Leonardo started a composition and then decided to make two paintings on the same theme.”

The painting went on view in the 2011 exhibition “Kings, Queens, and Courtiers: Art in Early Renaissance France” at the Art Institute of Chicago and at the Louvre in its 2019–20 blockbuster exhibition devoted to the artist, marking the 500-year anniversary of his death.

A prodigious collector, Griffin also recently sent 10 of his Jean-Michel Basquiat paintings to the Pérez Art Museum Miami, including the untitled 1982 canvas for which he paid a record-breaking $110.5 million at Sotheby’s in 2017.

“I’m delighted it’s come out into public view, because for a long time it was held pretty tightly to the chest by its owner,” Kemp told ARTnews. “It’s a little picture but of large-scale importance.”

Gagosian has closed its small space in London’s Burlington Arcade and will soon close up its space in Basel, Switzerland, the Art Newspaper reports.

Both spaces started as pop-ups, and as long as the rents were good, it made sense for founder Larry Gagosian to keep up those spaces, a source familiar with the gallery’s thinking told ARTnews. “Larry’s thinking is, ‘If there’s opportunity there, great. If not, that’s okay too,’” the source said.

Among the gallery’s London spaces, the Burlington Arcade location, which opened in 2023, was the smallest, with the downstairs featuring a store that sold books, editions, and other Gagosian merchandise. Upstairs was a tiny exhibition space that was closer to a private viewing room. Still, Gagosian managed to put on 16 shows there before closing up shop. But Gagosian isn’t abandoning London by any stretch. The gallery will continue to maintain its two Mayfair galleries, at Grosvenor Hill and Davies Street.

Basel followed much the same pattern as the Burlington Arcade space. Gagosian first took the space at Rheinsprung 1 as a pop-up around Art Basel in 2019. It wound up staying open for seven years and putting on 17 exhibitions. The gallery has said it is looking at other possibilities in the city, so another outpost in the city hasn’t been entirely rule out. 

The closure of these two spaces also doesn’t mean Gagosian is contracting. In New York, even as other mega-galleries trim their footprints, Gagosian recently opening a new flagship in New York. The new two-floor, 12,000-square-foot space combines the gallery’s operations from a former temporary space at 976 Madison and its two-level spaces upstairs in 980 Madison that it vacated earlier this year back to street level. Gagosian had maintained offices and galleries upstairs for decades before Bloomberg Philanthropies bought most of the building, forcing much of the operation elsewhere. 

Gagosian seems perfectly willing to admit when a location simply isn’t worth keeping, too. From 2016 to 2020, he had a space in San Francisco, but, as he told Elle Decor earlier this year, “It just failed. I mean, nobody showed up. It was so depressing.” He remembered flying in for openings only to find an empty gallery and wondering, in somewhat more boisterously colorful language, what he was doing there. 

The closures of two of Gagosian’s European locations come during a broader rethink of mega-gallery real estate. David Zwirner recently closed its townhouse gallery at 34 East 69th Street after nearly a decade on New York’s Upper East Side. The gallery said the move had long been planned and followed the completion of its expanded Chelsea campus, where Zwirner has increasingly concentrated its New York operations. It still has galleries on West 19th and 20th streets and at 52 Walker in Tribeca. 

Pace is making a more conspicuous cut. After layoffs and a substantial reduction to its artist roster, the gallery put its 8,600-square-foot Hanover Square location in London back on the market and is looking for something smaller.
